newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Pyongyang's submarine scare, blunder or threat?.
newsitem.headline: Pyongyang's submarine scare, blunder or threat?.

text.p: If it hadn't got stuck on rocks, mangling a propeller, the North Korean submarine that slipped through South Korean defences last month may well have glided home unnoticed, mission accomplished.
Instead, an alert taxi driver spotted the coning tower of the Shark-class vessel looming out of the darkness off a sandy beach.
The submarine is now at the centre of a crisis that brought Washington's top Asia official, Winston Lord, to Seoul last week to try to limit the damage.

Southern troops that clamboured aboard the vessel from inflatable dinghies were said to have found evidence it was on a commando mission -- maps, a heavy gun, an oath of allegiance to Pyongyang's Dear Leader Kim Jong-il.
South Korean President Kim Young-sam said the boat might have been dropping off assassins, or saboteurs, and warned the incident could lead to "all-out war".
And as it bobbed in the surf, the submarine was exhibited as proof that the North was still plotting to destroy its neighbour. Its 26 occupants fled to the mountains, where all but four were killed.
The United States gave the impression it was not quite so alarmed, raising the question: is South Korea making too much of a fuss?
Offended by such questions, Presdient Kim was reported by state radio to have snapped that if a hostile submarine turned up off Japan or the United States, war would break out.

And when U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher urged "all parties" to calm down, an angry Seoul media accused him of trying to play honest broker, instead of backing an ally. The State Department said Christopher had gaffed.

At a news conference on Saturday, Lord rounded on media reports of a rift between Washington and Seoul that he said were "highly exaggerated" and "misleading" and sent out a dangerous signal to North Korea.

But whereas South Korean officials demand punishment and emphasise the security threat, Lord stressed the need to keep engaging North Korea while conceding that "in the current climate it cannot be business as usual".
A joint U.S.-South Korea statement on the incident was designed to present a show of unity.

Both Seoul and Washington scoff at Pyongyang's assertion that the submarine drifted south because of engine trouble. Why didn't the crew send up an SOS, and surrender on the beach? Why were some dressed in South Korean army uniform?
Still, it was not the first armed intrusion from the North since the 1950-53 Korean War: there have been more than a score of them. Nor was it the bloodiest.
In 1968, 28 communist commandos were gunned down near the presidential Blue House in Seoul.
Among more serious outrages: the 1983 Rangoon bombing in which Pyongyang agents blew up 15 members of the South Korean government, including four cabinet ministers.

Some diplomats say Kim, barred by the constitution from seeking re-election, is playing up the communist threat before polls next year for his presidential successor. Red baiting is a sure vote-winner in South Korea. "It certainly doesn't do Kim any harm," said one envoy.
And the apparent ease with which the submarine evaded detection was a huge embarrassment to the military, demanding a grave response.
Privately, U.S. officials make clear they are exasperated by the escalation of hostile rhetoric between North and South Korea, according to senior Western diplomats in Seoul.

Washington fears spiralling tension will jeopardise its 1994 nuclear agreement with Pyongyang, the cornerstone of U.S. President Bill Clinton's carrot-and-stick policy towards North Korea and one of his major foreign policy achievements.
Lord insisted that the nuclear accord, which froze Pyongyang's suspected nuclear weapons programme, and an offer of peace talks with North Korea, were still good.
"We do not wish to isolate North Korea. South Korea does not wish to isolate North Korea," he said.
"We call upon North Korea to change course and change attitude. It's not too late to engage with the rest of the world."
